title: Supercharging developer workflow with Amazon Q Developer - Vikash Agrawal
talk_summary: A vendor demo of Amazon Q Developer walking through the SDLC: CLI/IDE/GitHub agents that plan, generate code, write unit tests, generate docs, run security scans, and debug deployed Lambda logs via AI Operations. It is almost entirely product marketing with no measured results, but a few workflow patterns (slash-command agents, issue-label-triggered PR agents, review-comment iteration, infra planning up front) are copyable.

takeaways.what_they_do: A GitHub agent is bound to repos and triggered by applying a label to an issue; it generates code, opens a PR, and reports when ready, all without leaving GitHub.
takeaways.evidence_quote: either use an existing issue or create a new one. Apply a label here... based on that issue, it will generate code

takeaways.what_they_do: Reviewers leave inline PR comments and request changes; the agent re-runs against those comments and updates the PR, so review feedback is machine-consumable.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can actually add comments and request changes like I normally would in a review and then request the changes. So it does it again

takeaways.what_they_do: A separate agent invocation (/test) reads the whole codebase and generates unit tests, including state-management cases, before the PR.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it was able to also understand the state and created relevant test for the state management itself

takeaways.technique: Plan infra/deploy up front in the plan phase
takeaways.what_they_do: The speakers' own retrospective: they skipped infra planning, hit a production import error, and concluded infra (IaC) should be generated during planning, not after coding.
takeaways.evidence_quote: one of the takeaways for me... is to think of infra upfront how your application is going to the customers

takeaways.what_they_do: An ops agent ingests a log group plus associated resources, builds a resource topology, and reports a root cause instead of a raw stack trace.
takeaways.evidence_quote: automatically starts looking at the log group and all the associated resources. It creates a topology and then figures out the root cause

takeaways.technique: Prompt planning as an explicit SDLC phase
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue prompt engineering should be planned alongside requirements, iterating on prompts before code exists.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the planning phase might probably also include planning your prompts because prompt engineering is going to be a very important skill set
